difficultyRationale: Requires weighing a genuine readability/maintainability trade-off rather than applying a simple rule like 'shorter methods are always better'.
explanation: Extracting a method is worth it when it gives a meaningful name to logic a reader would otherwise have to parse line-by-line, or when it enables reuse. Splitting single-use one-liners into separate methods purely to make each method short adds indirection -- jumping across the file -- without adding clarity or reuse, so it can reduce readability even though each individual method looks simple.

options.text: The second reviewer is simply wrong, because shorter methods are always more maintainable regardless of how they're used, even when a method exists only to shrink a line count and is called from exactly one place in the whole codebase.
options.explanation: Method length alone is not what drives maintainability; a short method extracted from meaningful, reusable logic helps readability, but a short method that exists only to shrink a line count and is called from exactly one place can hurt readability by forcing a reader to jump around.

options.text: The first reviewer is wrong -- methods should never be extracted unless the resulting method is reused in at least two places.
options.explanation: Reuse is one good reason to extract a method, but it is not the only one; extracting to give a well-named abstraction to a chunk of logic can be valuable even with a single call site, so a strict 'two call sites or never' rule goes too far in the other direction.

options.text: Both reviewers are equally valid opinions with no way to judge which design is better.
options.explanation: This isn't purely subjective: the trade-off can be evaluated by asking whether the split adds a meaningful name or reuse benefit that offsets the added indirection, which is a concrete criterion rather than an unresolvable matter of taste.

options.text: Extracting a method helps when it names logic a reader would otherwise parse line-by-line, or enables reuse; splitting single-use one-liners just to shrink line counts adds indirection without adding clarity.
options.explanation: This matches the internal-quality trade-off Fowler describes: good internal quality lowers the cost of future changes because a reader can find and understand what they need quickly. Over-extraction replaces one readable sequence with scattered single-use fragments, which can increase the cost of reading the code even though a metric like 'lines per method' improved.

references.title: Martin Fowler: Is High Quality Software Worth the Cost?
